extracted.intended_audience: students enrolled in MIT's Writing and Reading Short Stories (creative writing workshop) / anyone following the OCW syllabus
extracted.subtask_description: A semester-long creative writing workshop and readings course focused on the craft of the short story, including regular reading, in-class exercises, peer workshops, and production and revision of three finished stories. The syllabus defines attendance, submission, formatting, originality, and grading expectations for participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and close reading of assigned stories
rubrics_metrics.description: All stories are to be read by the first session of that week. Close reading and thoughtful reaction are crucial to developing a sophisticated sense of how various writers have addressed issues, and should inform participants’ original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read assigned stories and articles with a focus on technique (plot, character, place, theme). Even if you have read the assigned stories in a different context, read them again with a view towards technique and elements of style. Exercises during the week will focus on the particular element of style discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attendance and participation in class are essential to making progress as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department policy states that more than five absences will result in a failing grade. More than three absences may adversely affect your overall grade in this class. If you arrive more than ten minutes late to class, that will count as an absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop participation and critique preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Students will be required to prepare critiques for workshop, which will include thoughtful prepared notes on each piece presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participate actively in the workshop process, giving full and thoughtful responses to your classmates’ work. Missing a workshop is serious: you must still turn in all critiques to your workshop via email if you do not attend. Not attending your own workshop date, or not having material available to critique for a scheduled workshop will result in a full drop in grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of required stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Every student will write three short stories. Every student will be required to finish three pieces of fiction at the end of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each student is responsible for writing at least one piece that will be submitted to workshop and rewritten. The same piece can be resubmitted to workshop after substantive rewriting has been done. Major assignment due dates are specified (e.g., First story due Ses #10; first draft of second story due Ses #18; revised versions and story three due on listed sessions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive revision / rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: The same piece can be resubmitted to workshop after substantive rewriting has been done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised versions have specified due dates (e.g., revised Story 1 due Ses #22; rewrite of second story due Ses #25). Rewriting is an explicit part of the process and used to produce polished, finished fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises and exercise journal
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of exercises in the techniques discussed will be assigned; you will need to bring an exercise journal specifically for this class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises are designed to give students an opportunity to focus on different elements of fiction and to practice in those particular areas out of context. You will be doing exercises in class on a regular basis, especially in the beginning of the term, so always bring your journal and a pen/pencil. Selections from your journal and exercises should be typed; do not simply photocopy handwritten exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and submission format
rubrics_metrics.description: All work turned in for workshop will be typed, spell checked, and printed out double-spaced in black ink on white paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your name, class/section and the date go on the top in the right-hand corner. The title goes 3 lines down in the center. Number ALL pages in standard fiction format: Surname/TITLE WORD/page#. Turn in all work in hard copy to the instructor, and also upload work, exercises or critiques onto the course website under 'workshop' so the entire class has easy access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely upload and deadlines / late policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments must be handed in on the day due. All work must be uploaded by 9pm the night before the workshop is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handing in a story late will inconvenience your classmates and give them less time to prepare a thoughtful and useful workshop response. If there is an unavoidable reason for an assignment to be late, talk to the instructor or send email at least 24 hours before the due date to ask for an extension. Any final assignment handed in late without an extension, or after the due date of the extension, will cause a full drop in grade. No exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract grading baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor uses 'contract grading' meaning you are guaranteed to receive at least a B if you meet the contract conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To receive at least a B you must: attend class regularly; do all assignments and exercises seriously, with the full weight of your consideration, and on time; come to class prepared; participate actively in the workshop process, giving full and thoughtful responses to your classmates’ work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for A-level work
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements to receive an A are harder to quantify but include higher-level qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A-level work includes more sophistication and grace in the writing, lively storytelling, and prose that approaches publishable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and plagiarism policy
rubrics_metrics.description: All work in this class will be produced for this class. Do not use earlier work, or submit a story for this class that you are also submitting in another Writing class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism — using someone else’s language and/or ideas without proper attribution — is academically dishonest and can result in withdrawal from the course with a grade of F, suspension, or expulsion. Consult 'Academic Integrity at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology: A Handbook for Students' and the Writing Center’s advice on 'Avoiding Plagiarism.' When in doubt, see the instructor. It is better to hand in poor work than stolen/copied work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The reading will be mainstream literary stories, and the default assumption is that you wish to write in the same tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone who wishes to write in a genre other than mainstream is welcome to do so, but ought to identify the genre and be conversant with the tropes and conventions of the genre you choose; discuss with the instructor if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom electronics and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Laptop computers will not be open during class with limited exceptions; silence cell phones before class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: during Workshop to refer to stories online or notes, and on the last day of class for evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: All work produced for this class will be collected into a portfolio at the end of the semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and assemble your finished stories, revised pieces, and selected exercises/journal material for submission as the semester portfolio.
